Your first goal

From a repository that has never heard of Sigma to one goal merged by you, with a look at what was left behind.

On this page
  • The path
  • 1. Initialise
  • 2. Add one goal
  • 3. Run it
  • 4. The pull request and its review state
  • 5. Merge it
  • 6. What to look at in .sdlc
  • Drop-in or vision-first

Most people only need

  • Run /sigma-init once, and confirm the test command it detects.
  • Write one small goal with a checkable done when line.
  • Run /sigma-loop to take the goal through to a pull request. On the shipped defaults it opens the pull request and stops; it never merges. (/sigma-goal alone does not open one.)
  • You merge the pull request. The goal is recorded done after that, not before.

A goal is one piece of work with a line that says how you will know it is finished. Sigma takes it through research, plan, an adversarial review of the plan, implementation, review and a short retrospective, proves it with your test command, and hands you a pull request. This page follows one goal from a fresh repository to the merge. You need git, bash and python3, and the plugin installed for your host (Get started). A GitHub remote and a logged-in gh are needed for the pull request; without them, see On your own.

The path

1. Initialise

From the root of the repository:

/sigma-init

It checks git and gh, asks where the backlog lives, and detects your test command. It lists the candidates with a number and an id each; you confirm one by re-running with the pair it printed, for example /sigma-init --verify 1:<id>. Confirming is what lets a goal be proved: the verify command is what Sigma runs before it will call anything done. Add --demo to queue a throwaway goal that writes one note file, if you want to see the flow before writing a real goal.

QuestionPickWhen
Where do goals live?github (issues) or local-goals (files)GitHub is the default when origin is a GitHub repository. Local files need no account.
Which command proves it?Confirm a detected one, give your own, or declineDeclining leaves verify.enforce off, so a goal can be marked done without proof. Confirm one for a real goal.

Afterwards git status shows .gitignore and .sdlc/ as untracked. That is expected: commit .gitignore, .sdlc/goals/, .sdlc/project.md and .sdlc/config.json, and never ignore .sdlc as a whole (The .sdlc folder). The full list of what init does is on Setup. Run /sigma-doctor once to see anything missing.

2. Add one goal

Keep the first one small and checkable. A good goal names an outcome and one line that a command can confirm.

BacklogHow to add a goal
Local filesCopy the example file in .sdlc/goals/ to the next number, set status: pending (the example ships as proposed, which the loop never picks), and fill done_when with a checkable condition. The body is the goal, written as you would to a teammate.
GitHub issuesOpen an issue labelled sdlc:goal and assign it to yourself: the shipped config has no assignee filter, but /sigma-init in GitHub mode sets discovery.github.assignee to @me where it is unset, after which the loop works only issues assigned to you. Put a ## Done when section in the body with three to seven checkable statements. A goal without one is allowed on the defaults; it prints a warning and proceeds.
 
---
id: 0002
title: "Add a --version flag"
lane: auto
done_when: "running the tool with --version prints its version, and the tests pass"
auto_ok: false
status: pending
---

Add a --version flag to the command line tool. Print the version
from the package metadata and exit 0.

The example above uses the keys the shipped example file has; keep the keys your copy has and change only their values.

3. Run it

CommandUse it to
/sigma-loopWorks the backlog: pulls the next goal and runs it unattended through every phase, then the commit, the pull request and the post-pull-request review. On the defaults it stops at the open pull request. Anything needing a human is parked, not forced.
/sigma-goalInteractive. Drives one goal through the phases with your approval at every gate and ends by recording the outcome (done, or parked with a reason). It does not open a pull request. Use it to watch the phases once.
/sigma-goal <N> --landUnattended, for one GitHub issue: takes it to a merged pull request with no gate pauses. It needs work.enabled: true and work.auto_merge of protected or always, and refuses on the default off. Not for a first goal; see Running unattended.

Each goal gets its own git worktree and branch (under .sdlc/work/, on an sdlc/ branch cut from your base branch), so your checkout never moves while it works. Each phase prints a banner and a cost line as it ends. A run stops at the budgets in .sdlc/config.json; the shipped values are on Configuration. Check progress at any time with /sigma-status, or /sigma-log for the live trace of the goal in flight.

4. The pull request and its review state

Two shipped defaults decide what you see: work.auto_merge: off and work.require_review: changes.

SettingOn the defaults it means
work.auto_merge: offSigma never merges. It opens the pull request and leaves it. The goal is recorded as review, meaning awaiting merge: the issue stays open, the card (if you use a board) sits in QC, and /sigma-status and /sigma-doctor show how long it has waited.
work.require_review: changesAfter the pull request opens, a fresh reviewer that did not write the code reviews the real diff. A blocking verdict sends it back for a fix, a re-verify and another review, up to work.max_review_cycles times (3), then parks it for you. The gate also parks on a "Request changes" review or an unresolved review thread.

The loop posts its verdict as a comment on the pull request: sigma:approve to clear, sigma:block to stop. You can leave the same markers yourself, but they count only from the repository's owner, members and collaborators. A comment marker is not a human review: the loop's own account wrote the code and posts the approval, which GitHub cannot tell apart from an independent one. Treat the approval as one signal and read the diff yourself.

A goal can end somewhere other than a pull request. Parked means it needs a decision from you (see Troubleshooting); failed means it needs a fix. Without a usable remote, or with --local-only, there is no worktree, branch or pull request: the loop edits your checkout directly and records the outcome.

5. Merge it

Review and merge the pull request on GitHub as you would any other. The next time the loop looks (any pick, or the watcher's tick), it sees the merge, records the goal done and closes the issue. A goal is done only once its pull request has merged; recording it done earlier is refused.

Leave auto-merge off for the first goals

work.auto_merge has two other values, protected and always. Set them only once your base branch has branch protection that requires checks or an approval from a second person. Without that, nothing independent stands between an unattended merge and your base branch. See Landing: pull requests and merging.

6. What to look at in .sdlc

WhereWhat it tells you
.sdlc/goals/Local backlog. Each file's status moves pending, in_progress, done or parked.
.sdlc/state/review-queue.mdYour "needs a human" list: what was parked and why.
.sdlc/plans/, research/, acceptance/The written record of the goal: what it found, what it planned, and the done criteria it was held to. They travel on the goal's branch with the pull request.
.sdlc/journey/Local mode only: the audit trail of each phase. With GitHub issues the same notes are on the issue timeline.
.sdlc/state/log/The local action log, one file per goal, never committed. Read it with /sigma-log.

The rest of the folder is explained on The .sdlc folder; cost and timing per phase are on Cost and time.

Drop-in or vision-first

Both start the same way and share one spine, so you can move between them later.

Drop-in (default)Vision-first (opt-in)
Start/sigma-init, then goals against your existing code/sigma-vision, or /sigma-init --vision
Up-front workA thin .sdlc/project.md: stack and verify commandA tiered north-star in .sdlc/context/north-star.md: vision, strategy with non-goals, design, architecture
Effect on goalsNone beyond the loop itselfPlan review sends back a plan that contradicts your strategy or advances a stated non-goal. That is a review instruction, not a code check.

A drop-in project can add a north-star later. With none written, the alignment check does nothing.
